blocks.title: Abstract
blocks.content:
We develop an analogue for sphere packing of the linear programming
bounds for error-correcting codes, and use it to prove upper bounds for the
density of sphere packings, which are the best bounds known at least for di-
mensions 4 through 36. We conjecture that our approach can be used to solve
the sphere packing problem in dimensions 8 and 24.

blocks.title: Homogeneous spaces
blocks.content:
The space Rn is a 2-point homogeneous space; i.e., its isometry group acts
transitively on ordered pairs of points a given distance apart. By studying
packing problems in homogeneous spaces, one can put Theorem 3.1 into a
broader context, in which it can be seen to be analogous to previously known
theorems about compact homogeneous spaces.

blocks.title: Numerical results
blocks.content:
It is possible to get numerical results by using linear programming to
ﬁnd functions for use in Theorem 3.1, as was done for the kissing problem by
Odlyzko and Sloane in [OS]. The idea is to ﬁx one of f(0) and bf(0), and view
extremizing the other as an inﬁnite-dimensional linear programming problem.
One can try to approximate it with a ﬁnite-dimensional problem, and solve it
on a computer. Although we obtained some numerical results this way, it was
cumbersome and generally ineﬀective. Instead, we use the following approach.

Suppose S is a subset of Rn such that 0 ∈S, there are n linearly independent vectors in S, and for all x, y ∈S, the distance |x −y| is the square root of an even integer. Then the subgroup of Rn generated by S is an even integral lattice. Recall that an integral lattice is a lattice in which the inner product of each pair of vectors is an integer; it is even if every vector has even norm.

blocks.title: Uniqueness
blocks.content:
It is natural to ask whether the densest sphere packing in Rn is unique.
Of course, it is trivially not unique, since for example removing a single sphere
does not change the global density. However, it is conjectured that E8 and the
Leech lattice are unique among periodic packings. By contrast, in R3 there are
inﬁnitely many distinct periodic packings of maximal density. Our techniques
can be used to prove this uniqueness in 8 and 24 dimensions, given the following

Our methods are not limited to studying sphere packings, but instead
